title: End of the shift
note: Fictional unit and staff. Your unit’s spill card, exposure route, and the nurse in charge come first.
intro: You are an environmental service aide on the Saturday morning shift. At 11:20 you see a small pool of blood on the floor beside Station 6. The patient at Station 6 is still connected, and blood is dripping slowly from where the venous line meets the needle tubing.

choices.text: Tell the nurse immediately, keep people away from the spill, and wait for her direction.
choices.feedback: A patient who is bleeding comes first, and that is the nurse’s task. A spill at a station where a patient is connected is not yours to clean until the nurse says so.
choices.then: The nurse secures the connection. Once the patient is safe, she asks you to clean the spill.

choices.text: Tighten the connection where the blood is dripping, then clean up.
choices.feedback: Never touch tubing, the dialyzer, or the machine to “stop the leak.” You could open the line further. Call the nurse.
choices.then: The nurse arrives, secures the connection, and asks you to step back.

choices.text: Mop it up quickly before anyone slips.
choices.feedback: Mopping first leaves the patient bleeding and spreads blood. Tell the nurse; keep people away.
choices.then: You stop and call the nurse, who secures the connection.

vitals.task: Small spill, no sharps, away from patients

n2.scene: The spill is small, on the floor, with no glass or sharps, and the patient is safe. The nurse asks you to clean it with the spill kit.

choices.text: Sign out, gloves, apron, and eye protection; check for sharps; cover with absorbent from the edges inward; lift into an infectious-waste bag with the scoop; clean, then apply the disinfectant on the spill card and keep it wet for the full label time; dispose, remove PPE, hand hygiene, record, restock.
choices.feedback: Cleaning removes the blood; disinfection only works on a clean surface and needs its full contact time. Working from the edges inward stops it spreading.

choices.text: Pour disinfectant over it, wipe it up, and dry the floor.
choices.feedback: Disinfectant poured onto blood does not work well, and wiping it straight away skips the contact time. Clean first, then disinfect and leave it wet.
choices.then: You redo it following the spill card.

choices.text: Absorb it and clean the floor, then let the next shift disinfect.
choices.feedback: The disinfection is part of the same job, done now with the full contact time, and recorded.
choices.then: You finish the disinfection yourself and record it.

n3.scene: Turning over Station 9, you see an uncapped needle on the floor under the chair.

choices.text: Do not pick it up. Stand guard or put a warning sign over it, keep others away, and call the trained responder with tongs and a sharps container. Report where and when it was found.
choices.feedback: Do not pick up a loose needle even with gloves. A needle on the floor is a system failure upstream; reporting it helps the unit find out why.

choices.text: Pick it up carefully with gloved fingers and drop it in the sharps container.
choices.feedback: Gloves do not stop a needle. Most needlestick injuries happen exactly this way.
choices.then: The nurse sees you reaching and stops you. She removes it with tongs.

choices.text: Sweep it into the dustpan with the rest of the debris.
choices.feedback: A needle in a dustpan ends up in a general-waste bag, where it injures the next person.
choices.then: You stop, guard it, and call the nurse, who removes it with tongs.

n4.scene: The infectious-waste bag at Station 9 is nearly full, and you have more to add.

choices.text: Do not press it down. Tie it off by the neck, carry it away from your body, and start a new bag.
choices.feedback: Never press on bags or bins, never reach into them, never hug them. Hidden sharps in waste and linen are how support staff get hurt.

choices.text: Press the bag down to make room.
choices.feedback: A hidden needle can go straight through the bag and your glove.
choices.then: You stop before pressing, tie it off, and start a new bag.

choices.text: Hold it against your body to tie it tightly.
choices.feedback: Hugging a bag is another common needlestick. Carry by the neck, away from your body.
choices.then: You hold it by the neck instead.

n5.scene: Rinsing a basin at the sluice, blood-stained water splashes into your left eye. The unit is busy, and the nurse says, “It’s probably nothing; report it tomorrow.”

choices.text: Flush the eye with plenty of clean water now, tell the nurse in charge and your supervisor what happened and when, go to the unit’s exposure route at once, and complete the incident report.
choices.feedback: Wash, tell, go. A splash of blood into the eye is an exposure. For HIV, prophylaxis, if indicated, should start as soon as possible; hepatitis B steps depend on your antibody status. Doctors decide the medicines; your job is to get there quickly.

choices.text: Rinse it and report it tomorrow, as the nurse said.
choices.feedback: Delay matters: any preventive treatment works best when started early. An exposure is an emergency for you, even on a busy shift.
choices.then: You think again, tell the supervisor, and go to the exposure route that afternoon.

choices.text: Rinse your eye with the disinfectant from the spill kit to kill any germs.
choices.feedback: Never use bleach or chemicals on your eyes, skin, or wounds. Flush with plenty of clean water.
choices.then: You flush with clean water instead, report it, and go to the exposure route.

end.title: Next week
end.text: At the exposure clinic your baseline tests were drawn and the physician decided on follow-up. Your hepatitis B antibodies were protective. The unit traced the loose needle to a dropped cap during a busy changeover and added a nurse’s sharps sweep before stations are turned over. The exposure route is now posted in the staff room for contracted staff too.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • A bleeding patient is the nurse’s first. Never touch lines or machines.
  • Spills: contain from the edges, clean, then disinfect with the full contact time.
  • Never pick up a loose needle, even with gloves. Guard it and call.
  • Never press, reach into, or hug waste bags.
  • Exposure: wash, tell, go, the same day.
